analysis.one_liner: Replaces drug patents with government prize payments funded by a fee on health insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2013 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it received no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the legal monopolies — patents and marketing exclusivity — that let drug companies charge high prices, and replaced them with cash prizes paid from a government fund. Developers would be rewarded based on how many patients a new medicine helps and how much better it is than existing treatments, while any manufacturer could then sell it, driving prices toward generic-drug levels. The fund would be financed at about 0.55% of the economy each year, paid for by a fee on health insurers and federal appropriations.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who takes prescription drugs. Once a new drug cleared approval, any company could manufacture and sell it, so prices would fall toward competitive generic levels [S3]. Developers would be paid directly from a prize fund, with awards sized to patient benefit, therapeutic improvement, and priority needs like neglected and orphan diseases [S2][S3]. At least 5% of prize money would go to people who openly share research data and technology on royalty-free terms [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Strips the exclusive right to make, sell, or use any drug, biological product, or related manufacturing process, including patent-based delays that block generic competition [S3]

Pays innovators prize payments in lieu of monopoly profits, judged by number of patients helped, incremental therapeutic benefit, and priority needs such as global neglected diseases, orphan diseases, and infectious disease [S2][S3]
Guarantees minimum shares of prize money for priority research: at least 10% for orphan diseases and 4% each for global neglected diseases and global infectious diseases [S3]
Requires annual Government Accountability Office audits of whether the fund is delivering new medicines cost-effectively [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would pay an annual fee scaled to their premiums to finance the fund, exempting insurers with under $25 million in premiums [S3]. The fund would also be replenished by federal appropriations equal to 0.55% of GDP — more than $86 billion in 2012 terms [S3]. Brand-name drug and biotech companies would lose the exclusive sales rights that underpin their revenue, receiving prize payments of up to ten years instead [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and health insurers

drawbacks.text: The transition was abrupt: every drug already on the market would lose exclusivity on October 1, 2014, with prize payments capped so that fiscal 2015 awards could cover no more than 90% of the fund, leaving companies with sunk investments and no replacement revenue guarantee [S3]

A 13-member Board of Trustees would have enormous discretion to decide which medicines get prizes and how large the checks are — a government body picking the size of rewards that markets used to set, with the risk of underpaying breakthroughs or overpaying marginal ones [S3]

The financing is not free: the 0.55%-of-GDP fund (over $86 billion a year in 2012 terms) is paid by insurers — who typically pass costs into premiums — and by federal appropriations, and the insurer fee excludes government programs, so taxpayers would carry a large share [S3]

The model is untested at national scale: no country has replaced its entire drug patent system with a prize fund, and a badly calibrated fund could leave some diseases without a developer willing to invest

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential payoff is large: prescription drug prices in the U.S. are far higher than in countries where generic competition sets prices, and this bill attacks the root mechanism — legal exclusivity — rather than capping prices downstream. The costs are real but mostly transitional: drug companies would lose monopoly rents worth tens of billions a year and would have to trust an untested prize system to replace them. The honest case against is design risk — a panel of appointees sizing rewards for every new medicine is a gamble — but the bill's backers had a fair reply: the existing monopoly system already pays far more than $86 billion a year in excess drug prices. The bill got almost no legislative attention, so Congress never weighed these trade-offs on the record.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Sanders introduced it, the Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and the committee never gave it a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Introduced March 20, 2013, read twice, and referred to the HELP Committee the same day [S5]
It drew zero cosponsors in the Senate over its entire two-year life [S4]
No committee action, floor vote, or companion House action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their patent monopolies and premium pricing power, since nothing about the exclusivity system changed. Health insurers avoided the new annual fee. Patients continued paying monopoly-level drug prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept their monopolies

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin, D-IA, in the 113th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat after referral until the Congress expired

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only Senate action was referral, and no Democrat or Republican signed on as a cosponsor — support was a single Independent sponsor [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would end the patents and marketing exclusivities that let these companies set monopoly prices — the core of their revenue model. Their interest in keeping exclusivity runs directly against patients who pay those prices.

They would pay a new annual fee to finance the prize fund, but drug costs are a major driver of claims, so collapsing drug prices would cut their biggest expenses. Their net position depends on how the fee is passed into premiums.
With exclusivity stripped, any manufacturer could freely make and sell every approved drug and biologic, enormously expanding their addressable market.

Prize payments would replace monopoly profits for up to ten years, which could still be lucrative for breakthrough medicines but removes the outsized payoff that venture-funded biotech bets on, especially during the abrupt 2014 transition.
